newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan refugees still dying in their dozens.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees still dying in their dozens.

text.p: A United Nations airlift of Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire passed the 30,000 mark on Sunday but refugees are still dying in their dozens both in Zaire and Rwanda, aid officials said.

A further 1,700 refugees returned to the Rwandan capital of Kigali from the northeastern Zaire city of Kisangani on Sunday, pushing the total brought home to more than 31,000 since the airlift began in earnest on April 27.
Concern remains for the fate of tens of thousands more still in eastern Zaire as well as those who have already flown home.
Aid officials are concerned at a sharp increase in the death rate at a transit camp near Kigali set up to receive returnees.

Although the severe medical cases have been flown from Kisangani to a hospital in Gisenyi, 70 km west of Kigali on Lake Kivu, where the international medical charity Medecins sans Frontiers (Doctors without Borders) is operating, over 40 supposedly fit people have died at Runda transit camp near Kigali in the last five days.
"We have had nine confirmed cholera cases in the last days," said Faisil Tezera, head of MSF's Rwanda operation.
"We are also treating more people with bad wounds, injuries or other illnesses every day," Tezera added.
At Runda on Sunday morning, a tented morgue swiftly filled with the bodies of those who died overnight -- some from an MSF clinic and others from the camp proper.

"The refugees are supposed to be screened in Kisangani and only those fit to go home should be sent here," Tezera told Reuters. "But the reality is that they (aid officials) are overwhelmed in Kisangani and we are feeling that effect here."

MSF officials are now also screening the refugees when they arrive at Kigali's airport. The sick or injured are taken to a tented clinic and the rest are absorbed into Runda to await trucks to take them home.

"It is tragic that having made it back to Rwanda, they should die soon after," said a doctor at Runda. "I am not sure what conditions are like in Kisangani, but wouldn't it be better to get people well before they travel?"

Tezera said the number of refugees treated by MSF for inflicted wounds since the airlift began was fewer than expected. "We have only admitted 175 people into hospital for the kinds of injuries caused by machetes or guns," he said.
"This was low given the news reports we heard from Kisangani, but we do not have figures for those we treated but did not admit. Those are certainly higher."
Aid officials and journalists saw hundreds of refugees with gruesome wounds at Biaro camp, near Kisangani, after rebel soldiers and local Zaireans attacked the camp on April 21.
The Biaro refugees -- and those from nearby Kasese camp -- fled to escape the attack, but those that returned in the days that followed have been part of the huge U.N. airlift.

Officials fear that only around 40,000 of the camps' original 80,000 population have returned, and the rest are either scattered through the dense forests of eastern Zaire or were killed in the camp attack or during the days that followed.
The refugees were among over 300,000 who fled west from their camps in eastern Zaire rather than go home along with over a million others following the start of a revolt lead by Laurent Kabila.
The refugees originally fled their homeland to escape reprisals for the 1994 genocide of over 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
